title: Deterministic key sampling and TTL safeguard runbook for KV/prefix caches
creator: Aisha Patel
description:
Problem: We need a repeatable, low-risk way to propose and apply KV/prefix cache keying and TTL policy changes across hosted and dedicated deployments. Current experiments rely on ad-hoc sampling and manual rollback criteria, which makes it hard to surface regressions in tail latency, e2e token cost, and hit-rate distribution across multi-tenant workloads.

Goal: Build a deterministic key-sampling harness + TTL laddering safeguard that produces: (1) reliable hit-rate forecasts per-prefix, (2) synthetic unit-economics simulations (tokens saved vs. additional eviction cost), and (3) an automated staged-apply and rollback plan with concrete guardrails and observability hooks.

Scope: engineering-runbook + automation for: key normalization rules, deterministic sampling methodology, offline simulator, canary roll steps, metrics and alert thresholds, and an ops-oriented rollback automation. Produce artifacts: reproducible notebook, canary deployment job, and a template PR with suggested configs and rollback hooks.
acceptance_criteria: Deterministic sampler that given a seed + date range outputs the same sample of prefix keys for replay
Simulator produces per-prefix hit-rate and cost delta estimates and stores results to a dashboardable CSV/BigQuery table
Canary deployment plan with 3-stage ladder (shadow -> 1% -> 10%) and automatic revert if hit-rate drop > 5% or tail P99 latency increases > 20%
Runbook documents exact CLI commands and playbook for emergency rollback (time-bound autoscale throttle + config revert), with postmortem checklist
Integration tests that validate sampler/rewriter are idempotent and do not change produced cache keys for canonicalization rules
rollout_plan: 1) Offline: run deterministic sampler across 30d of traffic on prod shadow logs; generate per-prefix histograms
2) Simulate: feed sampled traces through simulator to compute token-saved / eviction-cost trade-offs and risk score
3) Review: PM/Eng/Infra review of top-20 high-risk prefixes with proposed TTLs and key-normalization changes
4) Shadow apply: enable new TTLs in shadow mode for 48h, collect direct hit/miss and tail latency metrics
5) Canary stage A: 1% traffic for 6h with automatic monitoring; fail if any guardrail breached
6) Canary stage B: 10% traffic for 24h; rollback automation enabled and monitored by oncall
7) Full rollout: staggered scaling to 100% via config ladder if canaries pass for 72h
metrics: per-prefix hit-rate (H) and delta vs baseline
token cost saved (tokens/sec) and estimated $/hour impact
P50/P95/P99 tail latency for inference requests affected by cache
eviction churn (keys/sec) and increase in cache lookups
slo breach count attributable to cache policy changes
safety_guardrails: automated preflight: require simulated hit-rate improvement >= 2% or cost-neutral with low risk score
hard aborts: revert if per-prefix hit-rate drops > 5% sustained for 15 minutes
tail protection: revert if P99 latency increases > 20% vs baseline within canary window
quota protection: prevent TTL reductions that increase cache storage > 15% without infra signoff
operator override: manual hold gate that can block rollout from 1%->10%
implementation_notes: Sampler: use deterministic hashing + reservoir sampling per-prefix so results are stable across replays; include seed in metadata
Canonicalization: fold numeric IDs vs free-text suffixes and preserve semantic segments (e.g., user:<id> -> user:<bucketed-id>)
Simulator: replay token-by-token to estimate KV hits/misses, apply batching model to reflect sequence-length correlated hit decay
Telemetry: emit per-key sample tags through request traces so we can attribute latencies and hits back to sampled keys
Rollback: implement a two-way toggle in config service with instant revert and a traffic-mounted safepoint to avoid in-flight inconsistencies
risks_tradeoffs: Overaggressive TTL shortening reduces operational cost but increases eviction churn; simulator must quantify churn vs savings
Key normalization can collapse distinct semantics causing cache pollution; choose conservative normalization rules initially
Sampling bias: low-frequency prefixes may be under-sampled; add stratified sampling to surface long-tail risks
Instrumentation overhead: per-key tracing increases telemetry volume; gate sampling to 0.1% baseline for continuous monitoring
